tagline: Wooded roads and rolling farmland follow an older trading corridor.
intro: The Historic Piedmont Scenic Byway runs through rolling farmland and the Oconee National Forest, crossing the Oconee and Ogeechee rivers. Its 82 miles combine State Routes 15, 16 and 77 with rural county roads in Putnam and Hancock counties. Georgia DOT highlights the route’s historic and cultural qualities, from Rock Hawk to antebellum homes. Narrow roads pass under trees before opening into farmland. The corridor plan describes the principal SR 16 leg and the northern loop as two-lane, two-way roads.

SR 16 follows the approximate route of the Okfuskee Trail, which connected present-day Augusta with the Mississippi River. Native Americans carried deer pelts along this corridor during the seventeenth century; families from Virginia and the Carolinas later traveled it into the Piedmont. The Eatonton Turnpike Company organized to make Eatonton the midpoint of the road between Sparta and Monticello. Later, the byway’s preservation goals joined its historical sites with the surrounding rural landscape.

Travel east from western Putnam County through Willard and Eatonton’s courthouse square, then cross the Oconee into Hancock County. The main route crosses Shoulderbone Creek and continues through Sparta to Jewell. A northern loop and roads toward Linton complete the byway network. Beyond Jewell, the separate Warren County-Piedmont extension follows SR 16 to Warrenton.
notice: Wooded stretches alternate with open farmland along the narrow roads.

moments.title: Rock Hawk
moments.text: Thousands of quartzite pieces form a large bird at Rock Hawk, but scholars do not know which bird its builders intended. The archaeological site lies off SR 16 on Wallace Dam Road, east of Eatonton near Lake Oconee. Rock Eagle, also in Putnam County, is the other known example of this kind of effigy mound east of the Mississippi. Rock Hawk is in poorer physical condition than Rock Eagle. A tall fence protects the mound itself from entry. Scholars have not established whether Rock Hawk suffered more degradation or Rock Eagle received more preservation or reconstruction.

moments.title: Shoulderbone Creek
moments.text: Shoulderbone Creek joins the Oconee River, and the community of Shoulderbone takes its name from the stream. At the SR 16 crossing, the Historic Piedmont Corridor Management Plan recorded an early-twentieth-century bridge with a view of Millmore gristmill. Millmore ground corn and wheat for two centuries. The same plan documented a treaty marker at the meeting of SR 16 and SR 77, with the Vinson-Harris-Lovejoy house across the road. SR 77 connects this part of SR 16 with SR 15 to form the byway’s northern loop, through wooded land with few visible residences.

moments.title: Sparta
moments.text: A New England house form appears in Sparta at the Rossiter-Little House: its main section follows a saltbox design. Timothy Wells Rossiter, a Revolutionary War surgeon from Connecticut, bought a lot at Broad and Miles Streets. The house departs from that regional pattern with two projecting front wings and a porch between them. It belongs to the Sparta Historic District, listed on the National Register in 1974. Sparta became Hancock County’s seat in 1797, two years after its founding. The present building incorporates an older log cabin, whose foundation remains beneath the crawlspace.
